incident_edges.relationship: Cooper’s labor history exposes colonial government’s categories and control over social relations
incident_edges.evidence_note: The primary Part I introduction, pp. 23–24, connects classifications of labor with colonial power. This records a particular social-political inquiry, not a claim that labor alone explains decolonization. The Mombasa case (234–241) now supplies a concrete sequence connecting mobilization, wage investigations, differentiated reform and repression.

named_group_routes.relationship: Coal and New World resources enabled divergence between comparably developed Eurasian cores (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pomeranz's own argument, The Great Divergence (2000), introduction (pp. 3–27 read; later-edition pagination). He takes 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?' as seriously as 'Why wasn’t the Yangzi Delta England?' and argues 'that Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path', a result avoided through 'sharp discontinuities, based on both fossil fuels and access to New World resources' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' than capital (p. 19). The Atlantic trade mattered for 'how much they relieved the strain on Europe’s supply of what was truly scarce: land and energy', and 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). The book uses 'the fruits of overseas coercion' to explain the difference from China and Japan, 'not the whole of that development' (p. 4). Cooper's 2000 review (read in full) summarises it in the same year: 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies', and objects that Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates'. The earlier Making of a Hinterland (1993) already argued, in the publisher's description, 'that the development of certain regions entailed the systematic underdevelopment of other regions'; Bianco (1996, p. 243, read) notes that it 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', including Huang's involution model. A contribution, not a founding: earlier arguments from colonial extraction (Williams 1944, Frank 1969, Amin 1974) are cited at p. 3, n. 2, and he notes parallels with Sugihara (p. 12). Huang's 2002 critique and Pomeranz's reply are later readings, not evidence for this edge. Revision 1.144: the critiques now have their own arrows (philip_huang → kenneth_pomeranz; economic → kenneth_pomeranz, which revision 1.145 moved to capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz, with Brenner and Isett drawn separately as robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz). Pomeranz restated the timing in 2003: "a gathering consensus, pace Huang, about the timing of that divergence" (JAS 62:1, p. 179, read). Catherine Hall reads the coal-and-colonies argument as part of "a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians": "Pomeranz sees the Atlantic slave-economy and the availability of coal as the two complementary factors allowing Britain to expand" (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, p. 24, read).

named_group_routes.relationship: Ecological constraint as economic history: hydraulic decay and deforestation in North China (1993) and land and fuel constraints across Eurasia (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The Making of a Hinterland (1993), checked at contents level: its chapters include 'Ecological Crisis and the Logic of “Self-strengthening”' (pp. 120–152), 'Sold Down the River?' (pp. 153–211) and 'Dealing with Disaster' (pp. 212–266), with appendices on 'Agricultural Losses from Hydraulic Decay' and 'Extra Transport Costs Incurred Because of Hydraulic Decay in Huang-Yun'. The publisher's description says it 'traces social, economic, and ecological change in inland North China'. Bianco's 1996 review (pp. 242–245, read in full) states that environmental degradation 'se taille la part du lion dans la démonstration de K. Pomeranz, qui consacre trois chapitres sur cinq au déboisement du Shandong occidental et au déclin catastrophique des travaux d'entretien du fleuve Jaune et du Grand Canal' (p. 243), and describes a population deprived of wood and burning straw, grass, roots and dung needed as fertiliser (p. 244). In The Great Divergence (2000) he says he writes 'much more' than Wong about 'environmental change' (p. 8, n. 13); chapter 5 offers 'a systematic comparison of ecological constraints in selected key areas of China and Europe' (p. 12); and shortages 'of fuel and building materials' and threats to soil fertility appear in all the densest cores (p. 20). Cooper (2000, read) calls it 'a neo-Malthusian, ecological approach that focuses on access to food and raw materials'. Bianco also judges that the 1993 book 'postule plus qu'il ne prouve' a deliberate strategy of selective development (p. 244). edge_267 stays: it is an undirected comparison of Cronon's, Worster's and Pomeranz's approaches between the two group entries, resting on the 2000 introduction only; this arrow is the person's directed contribution and rests chiefly on the 1993 book.

named_group_routes.relationship: Neo-Malthusian, Marxist and regional critics answer Brenner: the demographic historians misrepresented, 'political Marxism', doubtful England–France and east–west contrasts, class struggle narrowed to the countryside (1978–2004)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: This arrow represents the specified interventions of Postan and Hatcher, Le Roy Ladurie, Bois, Croot and Parker and Wunder in Past and Present (1978), and of Harman (1989; 2004) and Callinicos (1990); it is not a verdict of the group entry, which includes Brenner and his supporters. Postan and Hatcher: 'Both imputations are groundless' (p. 64). Le Roy Ladurie: 'somewhat superficial but also extremely insular'; 'simplistic assimilation between power (political) and surplus value (economic)' (pp. 101–102). Croot and Parker: 'Both halves of this argument are suspect' (p. 79). Wunder: 'fallen victim to the Prussian myth' (p. 91). Bois: 'radically disagreeing with his methodological orientation' (p. 107); 'a voluntarist vision of history' (pp. 115–116, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos 1990). Seccombe (1983): a 'tendency to deny the explanatory power of demographic phenomena'. Harman (1989): 'a very narrow view of class struggle'. Concessions kept: Croot and Parker, 'welcome and effective'; Bois, 'courageously attacks the Malthusian model'; Cooper, 'I sympathize with him'; Callinicos, 'a valuable corrective' (p. 111). The 1978 openings are read on Cambridge Core (1985 reprint pages); later pages are not quoted directly; the specified Bois passages (pp. 115–116) are mediated, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990).

named_group_routes.relationship: Class structure, not population or trade, decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth: serfdom in east and west, agrarian capitalism in England against peasant property in France (1976–82)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (whole article OCRed; the quoted pages 31, 47 and 75 read closely): 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends … and not vice versa' (p. 31); the two problems are east–west serfdom and 'the rise of agrarian capitalism and the growth of agricultural productivity in England in relation to their failure in France' (p. 47); 'the most complete freedom and property rights for the rural population meant poverty' (p. 75). Restated in 1982 as 'social-property systems' (Brenner Debate p. 213, Cambridge Core). A contribution within a contested line, not a founding: he writes that the view 'obviously derives from Marx's arguments' (p. 47 n. 40); Postan and Hatcher: 'The essentials of Robert Brenner's argument have been put forward many times before' (1985, p. 64); Cooper: he 'joins a long line of expositors beginning with the Physiocrats' (p. 138).

named_group_routes.relationship: Thompson's preface, which made class a relationship rather than a thing (1963; the wording on edge_924), is the text every round argued over: Johnson's 'culturalism' (1978, as Eley and Nield recall it), Cooper's 'people struggling not to be a working class' (2000), Eley and Nield's 'Thompsonian rhetorics of experience' (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The preface's wording is carried by the existing atlas record and edge_924 (the earlier reading was made in a transcription whose route is now excluded; the source's link is corrected in this revision and no new quotation from the preface is made here). Later readers, read for 1.152: Eley and Nield 2000, p. 24 ('the inspiration of Edward Thompson and Sheila Rowbotham'), n. 46 (the controversies 'brought to a head in Edward P. Thompson's anti-Althusserian diatribe The Poverty of Theory'), n. 47 (cultural Marxism as the first of 'three moments'), reply pp. 82–83 ('the rethinking from Thompsonian and similar models began' with 'experience'); Cooper 2000, p. 62 and n. 11 (Thompson 'wanted to show how the working class made itself, but never doubted that what was made was the working class'); the 2007 preface, p. v (the 'culturalism' 'Inspired by the influence of Edward Thompson'). Thompson's own critique of economistic Marxism stays on edge_924.

named_group_routes.relationship: Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) developed a related critique of labour-history categories through Bengal: 'Culture … is the "unthought" of Indian Marxism', an argument he distinguished from Thompson's; Chandavarkar's 1997 essay examined Thompson and Indian history (its previously recorded quotations await re-verification), Cooper used his 'abstract'/'real' labour distinction (2000), and Eley and Nield pointed to the South Asian exchange as where their discussion 'could easily be carried'
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Preface and introduction read in the existing atlas record (edge_916): 'an extended polemic against the reductionism' of political-economic analysis; 'Culture … is the "unthought" of Indian Marxism' (p. xii); 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5 n. 9). Cooper 2000, n. 4 (read): 'Dipesh Chakrabarty['s] distinction [of] "abstract" labor from "real" labor', used to argue that 'the general and the specific both have their uses'. Eley and Nield 2000, n. 2 (read): their discussion 'could easily be carried into African, Latin-American, and South Asian contexts. See especially' Cooper 1995 and Chandavarkar 1997. Chandavarkar's 1997 essay is carried in the atlas's existing reading of HWJ 43 (edge_916); its previously recorded quotations await re-verification and are not repeated here.

named_group_routes.relationship: With Frederick Cooper, distinguishes identity as a political/practical category from the analytical processes of identification, categorization and variable groupness.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Primary article opening pp. 1–2 and selected “In other words” / “Identification and categorization” section pp. 14–17 read in an explicitly identified OCR mirror. This is conceptual differentiation, not a dismissal of identity politics or all historical experience.

named_group_routes.relationship: With Cooper, analyzes the state’s power to impose classifications while distinguishing external categorization from people’s self-identifications.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Joint primary pp. 15–17: state resources support official categories, but states do not monopolize identification and categories do not automatically produce homogeneous groups. Historical examples/referenced authors were not independently audited.

named_group_routes.relationship: With Frederick Cooper, Brubaker questions Hall’s claim that identity remains analytically indispensable and proposes more differentiated terms for identification and group formation.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Beyond Identity, pp. 8–9. The jointly authored criticism explicitly recognizes Hall’s sophisticated anti-essentialism; it does not characterize him as a simple essentialist or deny the political legitimacy of identity claims. verification.note: Prior publisher check retained in history. Added primary preface xi–xv and title/imprint from publisher preview https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9780691188218_A33704825/preview-9780691188218_A33704825.pdf . Imprint states 1989 copyright and second printing/first paperback 2000; digital listing year is not original publication. Preface dated February 1988. Distinguishes culture’s logic from political-economic function, questions automatic capitalist homogenization, and advocates both equality and criticism of bourgeois individualism. Broad descriptions of Indian hierarchy remain the author’s contested claims. Book chapters, original mill records and Nair’s later-page examples not independently read; no whole-book or empirical adjudication. Addendum 2026-10-14: Publisher preview re-read for the 1.132 person entry, adding the introduction pp. 3–6 and acknowledgments pp. xvii–xviii to the preface. Quoted: 'my objective is to develop a critical understanding of these categories themselves'; the assumption about culture in Marx's 'capital' and 'labor history in general' (p. xi); 'an extended polemic against the reductionism'; 'Culture ... is the “unthought” of Indian Marxism' (p. xii); capitalism's 'need or capacity to homogenize' (p. xiii); 'citizen' and 'comrade' (p. xiv); the worker of Marx's assumption and the bourgeois notion of equality (p. 3); 'That my argument is not the same as Thompson's will be clear to any careful reader' (p. 5, n. 9); no 'working class' that runs 'in its empty sameness throughout the course of history' (p. 6). Eric Hobsbawm, Sumit Sarkar and others are thanked as readers of the manuscript (p. xvii). Chapters 2–7 remain unread.

verification.note: Review read in full in the Persée text layer, pp. 242–245 (Persée record etchi_0755-5857_1996_num_15_1; OpenAlex W2981359141: vol. 15, issue 1, pp. 242–245). The book is 'ambitieux, intelligent, informé, bien argumenté' but 'ne convainc pas tout à fait'; Huang-Yun, where the Yellow River and Grand Canal cross, covers roughly western Shandong (p. 242). Pomeranz 'ne sépare jamais l'enquête régionale du débat théorique', setting Huang's involution model beside the 'breakthrough' theses of Myers, Rawski and Brandt (the OCR reads 'Ramski'); central thesis: the state gave up its priority on reproducing the population and its regional redistribution, concentrating resources on competitive regions and sectors; the 'coût économique, social et écologique' for a region become peripheral 'au sens skinnérien' was extremely heavy; 'La dégradation de l'environnement se taille la part du lion dans la démonstration de K. Pomeranz, qui consacre trois chapitres sur cinq au déboisement du Shandong occidental et au déclin catastrophique des travaux d'entretien du fleuve Jaune et du Grand Canal' (p. 243). Tables and appendices estimate damage from deficient water control to agriculture, transport and trade; a population 'privée de bois' burns straw, grass, roots and animal dung needed as fertiliser; 'Il postule plus qu'il ne prouve une stratégie délibérée de développement sélectif'; praise for 'la remarquable monographie sur le contrôle des eaux du Grand Canal et du fleuve Jaune' (p. 244); chapter 2 on cotton and local social structure (pp. 244–245). A reviewer's characterisation of the book's contents, not Pomeranz's text.

sources.scope_note: In-period review: the 1993 book's ecological chapters, its regional-development thesis and a critique of its proof.

verification.note: Capsule review read in full on the Foreign Affairs page (dated 2000-05-01); Crossref 10.2307/20049750: Foreign Affairs 79:3 (2000), p. 162. 'Pomeranz takes a neo-Malthusian, ecological approach that focuses on access to food and raw materials.' The core areas of China, Japan and India 'shared similar levels of technological and institutional development with Europe by 1750'; 'Europe had more institutional slack, easier access to coal (which was crucial, in the author's view), and cheap imports of sugar and cotton harvested by slaves in its New World colonies.' Criticism: Pomeranz 'relies heavily on plausible guesstimates, based on extensive but fragmentary evidence, to make quantitative arguments', and does not mention Landes's Wealth and Poverty of Nations. A short review by an economist, not a historiographical assessment.

This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing'; the class-consciousness '"it" ought to have'; 'a cultural superstructure, through which this recognition dawns in inefficient ways'; 'a similar error is committed daily on the other side of the ideological divide' (Smelser, Dahrendorf); 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.'
